"executive_summary": "This study presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) and atoll source GX 9+9, using archival data from the Indian multi-wavelength observatory AstroSat. The authors combined data from two instruments — the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) — from a single observation taken on July 25, 2020 (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774). The source was found to be in the soft/banana state, as evidenced by its position in the hardness-intensity diagram (HID), which places it in the lower banana state. Spectral analysis was performed across three distinct flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3) over the broad energy range of 0.7–25 keV, with the best-fit model being const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb). The seed photons were assumed to originate from the accretion disk (diskbb), rather than from a blackbody surface, which failed to fit the data. Using the spectral parameters, the authors estimated the inner-disk radius (~16.57±1.29 km), the total unabsorbed flux (increasing from ~5.94×10⁻⁹ to ~7.30×10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² across the flux levels), and the inner-disk temperature. For the timing analysis, only LAXPC data were used due to its high timing resolution. A power density spectrum (PDS) analysis revealed broad-band noise (BBN)-like variability centered at ~0.1 Hz, with no quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) detected. The energy-dependent temporal properties were modeled using the formalism of Garg et al., which relates spectral parameters to physical parameters. The best-fit model (reduced χ² ~0.80) indicated that the variability originated from variations in the inner-disk temperature and the fractional scattering (fs), with a positive phase lag suggesting the perturbation moved from the disk to the corona. The findings suggest that the source is transitioning towards a softer state, as indicated by a slight decrease in the Comptonization temperature (kTe) and an increase in the inner-disk temperature (Tin). The study is constrained by the poor data quality of the single observation, and the authors emphasize the need for further multi-mission observations to better understand the source. The paper does not include a bibliography, so the top_influential_citations field is empty.",

"executive_summary": "This work presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) and atoll source GX 9+9, using archival data from the Indian multi-wavelength observatory AstroSat. The authors performed flux-resolved spectral analysis by dividing the data into three flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3), each spanning a narrow count-rate range, and fit the combined spectra with the model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) using XSPEC. They estimated source characteristics, including the inner-disk radius (~16.57 km), unabsorbed flux, and inner-disk temperature, and compared these with previously reported values. In the timing analysis, they used only the LAXPC data due to its high timing resolution and searched for quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and broad-band noise (BBN) features via a multi-Lorentzian power density spectrum (PDS) fit. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected, but a BBN-like feature was found centered near ~0.1 Hz. They then modeled the energy-dependent temporal properties of the fractional rms and phase lag using the propagative model formalized by Garg et al., finding that variations in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering (with a phase lag) explain the observed variability. The best-fit reduced χ² was ~0.80 for this model. The authors conclude that the source is transitioning toward a softer state, as indicated by a slight decrease in the Comptonization temperature (kTe) and an increase in the disk temperature (Tin) with rising flux. They note that the study is constrained by poor data quality and the limited availability of a single observation, emphasizing the need for further multi-epoch observations. The paper bridges observational data with theoretical models to interpret the radiative origin of the variability in a poorly studied atoll source.",

summary.title: Physics Frontiers: Bridging Theory and Experiment — Spectro-temporal study of atoll source GX 9+9 observed with AstroSat
summary.authors: Sree Bhattacherjee, Arbind Pradhan, Biplob Sarkar
summary.executive_summary: This work presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) and atoll source GX 9+9, using archival data from the Indian multi-wavelength observatory AstroSat. The authors combined data from the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) obtained during a single observation on 25 July 2020 (Obs. ID A09_018T01_9000003774). The source was detected in the soft/banana state, producing a disk-dominated energy spectrum across 0.7–25 keV. The authors performed flux-resolved spectral analysis by dividing the data into three flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3), each spanning a narrow count-rate range, and fit the combined spectra with the model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) using XSPEC. They estimated source characteristics, including the inner-disk radius (~16.57 km), unabsorbed flux, and inner-disk temperature, and compared these with previously reported values. In the timing analysis, they used only the LAXPC data due to its high timing resolution and searched for quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and broad-band noise (BBN) features via a multi-Lorentzian power density spectrum (PDS) fit. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected, but a BBN-like feature was found centered near ~0.1 Hz. They then modeled the energy-dependent temporal properties of the fractional rms and phase lag using the propagative model formalized by Garg et al., finding that variations in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering (with a phase lag) explain the observed variability. The best-fit reduced χ² was ~0.80 for this model. The authors conclude that the source is transitioning toward a softer state, as indicated by a slight decrease in the Comptonization temperature (kTe) and an increase in the disk temperature (Tin) with rising flux. They note that the study is constrained by poor data quality and the limited availability of a single observation, emphasizing the need for further multi-epoch observations. The paper bridges observational data with theoretical models to interpret the radiative origin of the variability in a poorly studied atoll source.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) and atoll source GX 9+9, using archival data from the Indian multi-wavelength observatory AstroSat. The authors combined data from the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) obtained during a single observation on 25 July 2020 (Obs. ID A09_018T01_9000003774). The source was detected in the soft/banana state, producing a disk-dominated energy spectrum across 0.7–25 keV. The authors performed flux-resolved spectral analysis by dividing the data into three flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3), each spanning a narrow count-rate range, and fit the combined spectra with the model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) using XSPEC. They estimated source characteristics, including the inner-disk radius (~16.57 km), unabsorbed flux, and inner-disk temperature, and compared these with previously reported values. In the timing analysis, they used only the LAXPC data due to its high timing resolution and searched for quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and broad-band noise (BBN) features via a multi-Lorentzian power density spectrum (PDS) fit. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected, but a BBN-like feature was found centered near ~0.1 Hz. They then modeled the energy-dependent temporal properties of the fractional rms and phase lag using the propagative model formalized by Garg et al., finding that variations in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering (with a phase lag) explain the observed variability. The best-fit reduced χ² was ~0.80 for this model. The authors conclude that the source is transitioning toward a softer state, as indicated by a slight decrease in the Comptonization temperature (kTe) and an increase in the disk temperature (Tin) with rising flux. They note that the study is constrained by poor data quality and the limited availability of a single observation, emphasizing the need for further multi-epoch observations. The paper bridges observational data with theoretical models to interpret the radiative origin of the variability in a poorly studied atoll source.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary identified during the Galactic center sounding rocket mission. It is an established atoll source that traces a 'C'-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram. Atoll sources exhibit two primary states: the hard/island state and the soft/banana state. The soft/banana state is further classified into upper and lower banana states. In the hard state, Comptonization dominates, while thermal disk emission dominates in soft spectra. Atoll sources show significant spectral changes over durations ranging from days to weeks. The rate of accreting mass is believed to increase from island to upper banana state. GX 9+9 is often detected in a luminous soft state with a ~220 mCrab X-ray flux in the 2–20 keV band. Spectral modeling is emphasized but often has geometric and locational ambiguities. The source is not a well-studied object, motivating new observational and modeling efforts.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to characterize the spectro-temporal properties of GX 9+9 using AstroSat data. The authors seek to compare the constancy between spectral and temporal analyses. They intend to estimate source characteristics such as inner-disk radius, flux, and inner-disk temperature. They hypothesize that the source is in the soft/banana state based on the hardness-intensity diagram. They hypothesize that spectral parameter variations with rising flux indicate a transition toward a softer state. They hypothesize that the observed broad-band noise variability originates from variations in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering. They predict that the energy-dependent temporal modeling will reveal a phase lag consistent with the propagative model.

Methodological Details
The study used a single AstroSat archival observation of GX 9+9 taken on 25 July 2020. The observation was analyzed using the LAXPC and SXT instruments of AstroSat. SXT and LAXPC data were used for spectral analysis, while only LAXPC data was used for timing analysis. LAXPC counters 10 and 30 suffered abnormal gains from 2018 onwards, so only LAXPC 20 data was used. LAXPC operates over a wide energy band from 3 to 80 keV. Good time interval data free from the South Atlantic Anomaly and Earth occultation was used to extract scientific level-2 data. The LAXPC software pipeline version Oct. 13, 2022 was used to extract scientific products. SXT works in the low energy range of 0.3 to 8.0 keV. The SXT data was processed through the AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b pipeline to generate cleaned level-2 event files. The SXT count rate exceeded the pileup threshold of 40 counts/sec during the observation. An annular zone with an outer radius of 13 arcmin and an inner radius of 2 arcmin was used to limit counts below the pileup limit. A 2% model systematic error was incorporated for the background uncertainty estimation. The SXT gain fit was applied with a slope of 1 and a free offset parameter. Both LAXPC and SXT spectra were optimally grouped using the ftool ftgrouppha. The spectral analysis was performed within the energy range of 0.7 to 25 keV. The spectral fitting was performed using the XSPEC package of HEASOFT version 6.31.1. The source flux was divided into three flux levels: FL1 (450–570 counts/s), FL2 (570–650 counts/s), and FL3 (650–770 counts/s). The parametric errors were estimated at the 90% level of confidence. The source distance was considered as 10 kpc for the inner-disk radius calculation. The disk inclination angle was considered as 60 degrees. The color-correction factor k was taken as 1.7.

Procedures And Architectures
The best-fit model was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), with the thermal Comptonization model ThComp used. A cross-calibration component 'const' was incorporated to calibrate the different instruments. The LAXPC 20 spectra were used as the base spectra, with its constant fixed at 1. The SXT constant was left free for the calibration. The ThComp model was an improved version of the nThComp model. The energy range was extended with 1000 log bins using 'energies 0.01 500 1000 log' for the ThComp convolution model. The covering fraction parameter of ThComp indicates the amount of seed photons that will be Comptonized. The optical depth was frozen at 9 to constrain the other parameters. Edge models were required at energy 2.4 keV to obtain a better fit. The inner-disk radius was calculated using the relation Rin = k2 (Ndbb /cosθ) 1/2 * D10. The total unabsorbed flux was estimated using the XSPEC model 'cflux' in the extended energy range of 0.01–100 keV. The timing analysis used a power density spectrum (PDS) plot to detect variability. The multi-lorentzian approach was used to the PDS to check for variability in different flux levels. The PDS was generated for the full flux in the energy range of 3–20 keV and a frequency range of 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz. The rms and time lag spectra were obtained using the LAXPC subroutine 'laxpc_find_freqlag' at the centroid frequency νo. The characteristic frequency νc was obtained using the relation νc = √(νo² + HWHM). The energy-dependent temporal modeling was fit in the rms and phase lag spectra using the model formalized by Garg et al. The model assumes a truncated disk and a hot electron plasma (corona) between the inner radius and ISCO. The best-fit model was the variation in kTin and fs with some time delay (phase lag) with respect to fs. The time lag was calculated using the relation time lag = phase lag / 2πf, where f is the peak/central frequency.

Key Results
The source was in the soft/banana state at the time of observation based on the form of the HID. The average inner-disk radius was estimated to be ~16.57±1.29 km. The total unabsorbed flux in FL1, FL2, and FL3 was ~5.94×10⁻⁹, 6.51×10⁻⁹, and 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻², respectively. The maximum flux reached 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻², comparable to 7.8×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² reported by [12]. The unabsorbed flux increased from FL1 to FL3. The inner-disk radius was relatively consistent with the previously reported value of 27±4 km by Iaria et al. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected in the timing analysis. A BBN-like feature was observed in a wide centered region as shown in Figure 3 (left). The PDS fit required two Lorentzians. The centroid frequency νo was ~0.04 Hz. The characteristic frequency νc was ~0.1 Hz. The half width at half maximum (HWHM) was approximately 0.09 Hz. The rms at ~0.1 Hz was increasing as the energy was increasing, whereas the phase lag was showing a decreasing trend with energy. The best-fit model for the energy-dependent temporal modeling gave a reduced χ² value of ~0.80. The combination of heating rate and optical depth gave insignificant χ² values (>2). The variation in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering, with a positive phase lag, explains the observed variability. The phase lag was 0.11±0.08, with δkTin = 0.56±0.10% and δfs = 81±32%. The slight decrease in kTe and increase in Tin across the FLs indicate a transition toward a softer state. The fractional scattering and change in inner-disk temperature are the causes of the obtained broad-band noise variability.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The source is transitioning toward a softer state, as indicated by a slight decrease in kTe and an increase in Tin across the flux levels. The observed variability originates from variations in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering, with the perturbation moving toward the coronal region. The positive phase lag indicates that the variation in the fraction of seed photons being Comptonized follows the variation in the inner-disk temperature. The propagative model formalized by Garg et al. successfully explains the energy variability in the observed source. The best-fit reduced χ² of ~0.80 supports the validity of the energy-dependent temporal model. The model relates spectral parameters with physical parameters, helping to understand the factor leading to stochastic variability. The variation in the inner-disk temperature was initially introduced, and the perturbation moved toward the coronal region. The spectral and temporal analyses are consistent, supporting the constancy between them.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is constrained due to poor data quality of the source. The source is not a well-studied object, limiting the interpretation of the results. Only a single observation was available, limiting the statistical robustness of the analysis. The phase lag cannot be reliably used due to consistent error bars within the data points. The difference between the peak in the spectra and the ν₀ of the Lorentzian is more pronounced in BBN features than in QPOs. The variation in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering were the only variations considered, due to bad χ² values for additional variations. The inner-disk radius estimate is relatively consistent with the previously reported value, but the exact values differ. The maximum flux reached 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻², which is comparable to but not identical to the previously reported value. The study assumes a distance of 10 kpc, which is within the range of 5 kpc and 10 kpc. The disk inclination angle was considered as 60 degrees, which is within the range of previously reported values.

The source GX 9+9 was in the soft/banana state during the observation, producing a disk-dominated energy spectrum. The source was in BS at the time of observation based on the form of HID. The disk thermal emission is more prominent in soft spectra. The best-fit model included a diskbb component. The source is not a well-studied object, limiting the confidence in the state classification. The soft/banana state classification supports the disk-dominated spectral model. The state classification is consistent with the higher luminosity of the source.

The variability interpretation supports the propagative model formalized by Garg et al. The variability interpretation helps to understand the factor leading to stochastic variability in the system.

Data And Code Availability
The data used in this study is archival AstroSat data, which is publicly available. The analysis was performed using the standard pipelines and software of AstroSat, LAXPC, and SXT.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The best-fit model was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), which gave a good fit with physical spectral parameters. The blackbody surface model was unable to explain the observational data with a reducedχ2 value > 2. The combination of heating rate and optical depth gave insignificant χ² values (>2). The best-fit model was the variation in kTin and fs with some time delay (phase lag) with respect to fs. The variation in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering were the only variations considered, due to bad χ² values for additional variations. The best-fit model was comparable to the one employed by Chatterjee et al. [16]. The ThComp model was an improved version of the nThComp model. The edge models were required at energy 2.4 keV to obtain a better fit.

Ethical Considerations
The study used archival AstroSat data, which is publicly available and does not require ethical approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the HID of the source using the AstroSat data, with a binning time of 32s. Each color in Figure 1 represents the different flux levels as indicated in the plot. Figure 2 shows the best-fit spectrum of FL1, FL2, and FL3 from top to bottom, in the energy range 0.7-25 keV. The red and black points in Figure 2 represent the SXT and LAXPC 20 data, respectively. Figure 3 (left) shows the PDS fit, and Figure 3 (right) shows the energy dependent temporal modelling of fractional rms and phase lag. Table 1 displays the best-fit parameters of spectral analysis and energy-dependent temporal modeling. The best-fit parameters include NH, kTe, fs, Tin, Ndbb, Rin, and χ²/dof for each flux level.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the spectro-temporal characterization of the poorly studied atoll source GX 9+9 using AstroSat data. 2. The strongest evidence is the best-fit reduced χ² of ~0.80 for the energy-dependent temporal model, supporting the variability interpretation. 3. The future path is further multi-epoch observations to improve the understanding of the source and validate the variability interpretation.
